title: Apocrypha rejected for never being in the Canon
source_text: XXXIII. Ultro quidem concedimus Doctores Ecclesiae antiquae eo nomine rejecisse libros Apocryphos, quos haeretici confinxerant, & pro divinis obtrudebant, quod libri illi nunquam in Canone Ecclesiae fuerint, neque a Doctoribus Ecclesiae agniti, & pro divinis habiti & citati. Et hanc eorum argumentationem tanquam legitimam probamus, & simili plane modo impugnamos authoritatem librorum illorum quos Ecclesia Romana adjicit ad Vetus Testamentum supra Ecclesiae Judaicae Canonem: nempe, quia hi libri nunquam ab Ecclesia Judaica agniti fuerunt, etiam tum quum vera & sola esset Dei Ecclesia. Imo nec a primitiva Ecclesia Christiana, cujus Doctores communi consensu, paucissimis forte quibusdam exceptis, libros illos e Canone expungunt, licet eorum lectionem in Ecclesiis admittant, tanquam utilem ad plebis aedificationem. Et quamvis libri plerique Apocryphi notas quasdam in se vanitatis habeant, & infirmitatis humanae vestigia, quibus deprehendi possit illos a Deo inspiratos non esse: tamen absolute & in genere loquendo, non putamus ullum esse magis idoneum argumentum, quo librorum Apocryphorum authoritas infringi possit, quam quod nunquam vera Dei Ecclesia eos pro divinis habuerit.
pass_a_gloss: We freely indeed concede that the Doctors of the ancient Church rejected on that ground the Apocryphal books which heretics had forged and were thrusting forward as divine, because those books never were in the Canon of the Church, nor were acknowledged by the Doctors of the Church and held and cited as divine. And we approve that argumentation of theirs as legitimate, and in a plainly similar way we attack the authority of those books which the Roman Church adds to the Old Testament above the Canon of the Jewish Church: namely, because these books were never acknowledged by the Jewish Church, even then when it was the true and only Church of God. Indeed not even by the primitive Christian Church, whose Doctors by common consent, a very few perhaps excepted, expunge those books from the Canon, although they admit their reading in the Churches as useful for the edification of the people. And although most of the Apocryphal books have in themselves certain marks of vanity, and traces of human weakness, by which it can be detected that they were not inspired by God: yet absolutely and speaking in general, we do not think there is any more suitable argument by which the authority of the Apocryphal books can be broken than that the true Church of God never held them as divine.
pass_b_english: We gladly grant that the doctors of the ancient Church rejected the apocryphal books heretics had forged and pushed as divine on this ground: those books were never in the Church's Canon, nor acknowledged, held, and cited as divine by the Church's doctors.

We treat that argument as sound, and we use the same kind of argument against the books Rome adds to the Old Testament beyond the Jewish Canon — because the Jewish Church never acknowledged them, even while it was still God's true and only Church.

Nor did the primitive Christian Church: its doctors, by common consent (a very few perhaps excepted), remove those books from the Canon, though they allow them to be read in churches as useful for the people's edification.

Many apocryphal books do carry marks of vanity and traces of human weakness that show they are not God-inspired. Still, speaking absolutely and in general, we judge no argument more fit to break their authority than this: the true Church of God never held them as divine.
